questions.question: A model answers from policies that change every week. What should the first production baseline usually test?
options: Full-parameter fine-tuning on last month's policy text
Retrieval with current sources, citation checks, and a prompt baseline
More epochs on the existing dataset
A larger LoRA rank without a held-out set
questions.explanation: Frequently changing facts belong in a versioned retrieval path first. Fine-tuning can shape behavior, but it does not keep facts current by itself.

questions.question: Why should near-duplicate records be grouped before train and test splitting?
options: To guarantee that training loss reaches zero
To make tokenization independent of the base model
To stop the evaluation set from repeating content the model effectively saw during training
To remove the need for slice metrics
questions.explanation: Record-level random splits can place variants of the same source in both sets and inflate the apparent generalization result.

questions.question: Which formatting contract must stay aligned from SFT data to serving?
options: Only the visible user prompt
Only the number of training epochs
The accelerator model used for training
Base checkpoint, tokenizer, chat template, special tokens, truncation, and loss mask
questions.explanation: Changing tokenization or role boundaries changes the token sequence the model receives and can invalidate a trained adapter.

questions.question: When is LoRA a strong first fine-tuning baseline?
options: When the target is stable behavior and the team needs a small, reversible task artifact
When facts change hourly and no retrieval system exists
When the task rubric has not been defined
When the team wants guaranteed parity with full fine-tuning
questions.explanation: LoRA reduces the trainable and stored parameter surface, but quality must still be measured against a full-fine-tune or prompting baseline when relevant.

questions.question: Training loss keeps falling while validation loss and rare-slice quality worsen. What is the sound response?
options: Always deploy the final epoch because it has the lowest training loss
Remove the rare slice from the release gate
Inspect an earlier checkpoint, reduce optimization pressure, and review the data distribution
Increase the learning rate until validation follows training
questions.explanation: Diverging held-out evidence is an overfitting signal. Checkpoint selection is a release decision, not a last-step convention.

questions.question: Why is an adapter file alone not a complete release artifact?
options: Adapters contain no trainable weights
It depends on the exact base model, tokenizer, template, target modules, and adapter configuration
Adapters can run on any architecture after renaming the file
Adapters always require the original training dataset at inference time
questions.explanation: An adapter is a delta against a declared base and formatting contract. Lineage and compatibility are part of correctness.

questions.question: A candidate improves the aggregate task score but fails a safety slice. What should the release gate do?
options: Average safety into the aggregate and release if the mean rises
Deploy to all traffic and monitor later
Discard the base-model comparison
Hold the release and investigate the slice regression
questions.explanation: Critical slice and safety gates should remain independent so aggregate gains cannot hide a release-blocking regression.

questions.question: What should a rollback record identify for a fine-tuned release?
options: The previous model or adapter alias plus its base, tokenizer, template, prompt, and serving configuration
Only the training job duration
Only the current checkpoint hash
The author of the first prompt example
questions.explanation: Rollback must restore a compatible system configuration, not merely swap one weight file.
